title: Sisi Moves to Put Egyptian Forces Behind Saudi Arabia as Houthi Strikes Close In on Riyadh, Trump Freezes Russia Sanctions for 60 Days, and Ukraine's Allies Walk Out of the IMF
subhead: Egypt's president asked parliament for authority to send defence assistance to Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks killed 14 at Riyadh's main airport. In Washington, Rubio confirmed a 60-day waiver of newly passed Russia sanctions; in Bangkok, Western finance chiefs walked out on Moscow's minister.

sections.heading: Egypt Offers to Defend Saudi Arabia
sections.body:
President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called an emergency parliamentary session on Saturday to authorise him to approve any Saudi request for defence assistance, Al Jazeera reports. At a Military Academy graduation in Cairo he said Egypt would 'carry out any measure to protect' Saudi Arabia and that he was 'not speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. I am speaking only for defence.'

The trigger is concrete: Houthi attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport earlier this month killed 14 people and wounded more than 300, per Al Jazeera, with further strikes reported on Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran. The kingdom's own anti-Houthi campaign — launched this month by Yemen's internationally recognised government — is now running alongside Gulf air operations against the Houthi siege of Taiz (Saudi-led forces say they struck multiple positions in the city, Al Jazeera).

Egyptian forces have not fought in Yemen since the 1960s, and Sisi's framing is defensive, not expeditionary. What matters is the direction of travel: a second Arab army openly pricing in involvement in a war that is currently hitting Saudi airports and oil infrastructure. Egyptian officials have also described Saudi and Gulf security as 'an integral part of Egypt's national security'.
sections.whyItMatters: An Egyptian commitment on Saudi territory would turn a Yemen-Saudi exchange of fire into a wider Arab coalition problem, and would do so while the US is already stretched across Iran and the Gulf. It also gives Riyadh a ground-mobility option it has not had all year.

sections.heading: Three Tankers Burn and Two Governments Claim the Same Strait
sections.body:
Iran's navy said an oil tanker caught fire in the Sea of Oman after the IRGC reported a second supertanker struck a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, according to Al Jazeera's live coverage. The IRGC says the two vessels, each carrying roughly two million barrels of crude, used an 'unauthorised' route outside its Persian Gulf Strait Authority system.

Washington's version is different. CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper said the strait 'is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran', and that 400 ships and 100 million barrels moved through in the past week; the US military maintains its minesweepers have cleared the waterway and that vessels are being hit by IRGC projectiles. UKMTO counted at least 12 vessels attacked in the week to October 16 alone, and warned that most victims never report, so the true count is higher.

The market is already pricing the gap between those two accounts. Kpler data cited by Al Jazeera puts Hormuz flows at 11.6 million barrels per day in the week to October 13 — about 68 percent of the 17.1 million bpd pre-war baseline — and Brent touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May.
sections.whyItMatters: The dispute is not really about who controls the strait — it is that a third of normal oil flow has been missing for weeks and neither side claims responsibility for making it safe. Both the IRGC and CENTCOM are describing an open, contested waterway in the same week.

sections.heading: Trump Freezes New Russia Sanctions for 60 Days
sections.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump's decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia — including restrictions Congress had recently passed — will last 60 days, and that the White House will 'analyze' the global impact, France 24 reports. The BBC reports the waiver covers many of the new congressional restrictions and was justified on national security grounds.

Reaction has been sharp on both fronts. Zelensky called the move a reward for Putin and warned it would embolden him and intensify the war, according to The Guardian, which also reported that Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine's power plants. Reuters via SBS and Al Jazeera report bipartisan US criticism and growing expectation in Kyiv that more relief could follow. Moscow, per France 24, has called the waiver 'historic'.

The European response was visible at the IMF meetings in Bangkok: Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey walked out of a session along with counterparts from France, Germany and several Nordic and Baltic states when Russia's finance minister, Anton Siluanov, took the floor (The Guardian).
sections.whyItMatters: A 60-day waiver is a clock, not a policy. It gives Moscow a defined window to bank relief, gives Kyiv and European capitals a defined window to reverse it, and puts an IMF meeting at the centre of the transatlantic split.

sections.heading: Settlers Attack EU Diplomats in the West Bank
sections.body:
Masked Israeli settlers attacked a European diplomatic delegation during the olive harvest in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, assaulting a French mayor and damaging vehicles, Al Jazeera reports; the delegation included officials from Belgium and Poland. Trump-appointed US ambassador Mike Huckabee called a separate attack on an American journalist a 'despicable act of terror' and urged Israel to prosecute, per Al Jazeera.

It comes the same week the UN Security Council held an open debate on the Occupied Palestinian Territory amid what UN News described as a rise in lethal Israeli strikes, demolitions and violence in Gaza and the West Bank. UNICEF reported on Friday that more than 340 children have been killed in Gaza in the year since the ceasefire was announced.

Separately in Cairo, Fatah and Hamas concluded a second round of intra-Palestinian dialogue under Egyptian sponsorship on Saturday, with Fatah's Monzer al-Hayek calling the talks positive and aimed at Palestinian unity on a PLO-based programme (Xinhua).
sections.whyItMatters: Attacks on EU diplomats turn a consular irritant into a European political problem, and they land while Washington's own ambassador is publicly pressing Jerusalem on settler violence. Cairo is meanwhile trying to convert its mediation role into Palestinian reconciliation — a lever it needs if it is to send forces toward Saudi Arabia.

sections.heading: NATO's Black Sea Problem Has a Turkish Lock
sections.body:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the territorial waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania pushed the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security, RFI reports. At least seven crew members were reported missing after the latest drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea. Any allied naval response, however, depends on Turkey reversing its refusal to admit warships into the Black Sea — a restriction rooted in the Montreux Convention.

Turkey has kept that line through the entire war. The attacks are now within NATO waters rather than Ukraine's, which is precisely the category Ankara has argued it can avoid.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the one place where an allied escalation is blocked not by Russia but by a member state's own treaty position. If attacks inside Bulgarian and Romanian waters continue, the pressure on Ankara becomes hard rather than diplomatic.

sections.heading: Addis Ababa Installs a Caretaker in Tigray
sections.body:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray on Friday and promised elections at the end of it, Reuters and France 24 report; ENA, the state news agency, confirmed the caretaker body was established on October 16. The move follows federal forces pushing back a TPLF uprising that began in September and revived the 2020-2022 war.

The wider regional picture is worse: Ethiopia has closed its embassy in Eritrea and expelled ten Eritrean diplomats, accusing Asmara of financing the TPLF, and Eritrea responded by severing diplomatic ties entirely (AP, Reuters). An Egyptian diplomat was also declared persona non grata in Addis Ababa.
sections.whyItMatters: A caretaker government and a six-month election promise is a claim of control, not a settlement — the TPLF has not agreed to it. Ethiopia and Eritrea are now formally without diplomatic relations while both are fighting inside Tigray.

bottomLine: The day's common thread is Gulf and allied capacity being asked to cover more ground at once: Egypt pricing in defence of Saudi Arabia, NATO unable to move ships into the Black Sea without Turkey, and a US administration giving Moscow a 60-day sanctions pause while still policing Hormuz. The concrete numbers are the ones to watch — 11.6 million barrels a day through Hormuz against a 17.1 million pre-war baseline, Brent near $110, 60 days on the Russia waiver, six months on Tigray's promised election.
